rows.question: What is the punishment for defamation?
queries: What is the punishment for defamation?
punishment for defamation criminal offence imputation concerning any person
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita section 356 punishment for defamation

rows.answer:
The punishment for defamation is simple imprisonment for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both, or with community service, under Section 356 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, which replaced Section 500 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 [1][8].

Conditions and time limits:
- The offence of defamation is non-cognizable and bailable, and is triable by any magistrate [5].
- Except when instituted upon a complaint made by the public prosecutor in specific cases involving public servants or high dignitaries, no court shall take cognizance of the offence except upon a complaint made by some person aggrieved by the offence, under Section 222 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (which replaced Section 199 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973) [4][10].
- When a complaint concerning public functions is made by the public prosecutor regarding the President, Vice-President, Governor, Administrator, or a Minister or public servant, the complaint must be made within six months from the date on which the offence is alleged to have been committed, under Section 222 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 [4].

rows.question: When can a person accused of a non-bailable offence be released on bail?
queries: When can a person accused of a non-bailable offence be released on bail?

rows.answer:
A person accused or suspected of the commission of a non-bailable offence may be released on bail by an officer in charge of a police station or by a Court other than the High Court or Court of Session, except where there appear reasonable grounds for believing they have been guilty of an offence punishable with death or imprisonment for life, or where the offence is a cognizable one and they have a previous conviction for an offence punishable with death, imprisonment for life, or imprisonment for seven years or more, or two or more previous convictions for a cognizable offence punishable with imprisonment for three years or more but less than seven years, under Section 480 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (which replaced Section 437 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973) [1][3].

Conditions and time limits:
- The Court may direct the release of a person otherwise barred under the specified clauses if such person is a child, a woman, sick, or infirm [1].
- The Court may direct the release of a person with prior convictions if satisfied it is just and proper for any other special reason [1].

rows.question: What is the notice period before filing a cheque bounce complaint?
queries: What is the notice period before filing a cheque bounce complaint?
notice period for payment of amount of money after dishonour of cheque
The Negotiable Instruments Act 1881 section 138 notice demand payment
dishonour of cheque for insufficiency of funds cause of action limitation period
topSources: The Indian Limitation Act 1908, 9 of 1908 (Rep., Act 36 of 1963) s1
rows.answer:
A demand for payment by giving a written notice must be made within thirty days of the receipt of information from the bank regarding the return of the cheque as unpaid, under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 [1].

Conditions and time limits:
- The cheque must be presented to the bank within a period of six months from the date on which it is drawn or within the period of its validity, whichever is earlier, under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 [1].
- The written notice demanding payment must be given within thirty days of the receipt of information by the payee or holder in due course from the bank regarding the return of the cheque as unpaid, under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 [1][12].
- The drawer of the cheque is given fifteen days from the date of receipt of the notice to make the payment, under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 [1][12].

rows.question: What is presumed about consideration for a negotiable instrument?
queries: What is presumed about consideration for a negotiable instrument?
presumption as to negotiable instruments consideration date time stamp acceptance transfer holder
Negotiable Instruments Act section 118 presumption as to consideration
Negotiable Instruments Act section 138 presumption in favour of holder
rows.answer:
Every negotiable instrument was made or drawn for consideration, and every such instrument, when it has been accepted, indorsed, negotiated or transferred, was accepted, indorsed, negotiated or transferred for consideration, under Section 118 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 [1]. 

As discussed by the Supreme Court in K.P.O. Moideenkutty Hajee versus Pappu Manjooran and Anr., Section 118(a) of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 imposes a duty on the court to raise a presumption that the negotiable instrument was made for consideration, which shifts the burden of proof to the defendant to establish that the instrument is not supported by consideration [1].

Related provisions:
- Section 43 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, which states that a negotiable instrument made, drawn, accepted, indorsed or transferred without consideration, or for a consideration which fails, creates no obligation of payment between the parties to the transaction [6].

I couldn't find any other specific statutory conditions or time limits regarding this presumption in the Acts I searched.

rows.question: When can a contract be avoided if consent was obtained by coercion or misrepresentation?
queries: When can a contract be avoided if consent was obtained by coercion or misrepresentation?
contract voidable on account of coercion fraud misrepresentation
Indian Contract Act section 19 voidability of agreements without free consent
Indian Contract Act section 15 coercion defined and section 18 misrepresentation defined
rows.answer:
A contract is voidable at the option of the party whose consent was caused by coercion, fraud, or misrepresentation under Section 19 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 [1]. 

A contract is not voidable if consent was caused by misrepresentation or by fraudulent silence, and the party whose consent was so caused had the means of discovering the truth with ordinary diligence, as stated in the Exception to Section 19 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 [1].

Related provisions:
- Section 19A of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 provides for setting aside contracts induced by undue influence [4].

rows.question: Who is competent to enter into a contract?
queries: Who is competent to enter into a contract?
competency to contract age of majority soundness of mind disqualified by law
Indian Contract Act section 11
Indian Contract Act section 12 mental capacity soundness of mind for contract
topSources: The Indian Council of World Affairs Act, 2001 s1
rows.answer:
Every person is competent to contract who is of the age of majority according to the law to which he is subject, who is of sound mind, and who is not disqualified from contracting by any law to which he is subject, as stated in Section 11 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 [1][12].

Related provisions:
- Section 10 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, which provides that all agreements are contracts if they are made by the free consent of parties competent to contract, for a lawful consideration and with a lawful object, and not expressly declared to be void [6][12]

rows.question: What is the punishment for murder?
queries: What is the punishment for murder?

rows.answer:

When a group of five or more persons acting in concert commits murder on the ground of race, caste or community, sex, place of birth, language, personal belief or any other similar ground, each member of such group shall be punished with death or with imprisonment for life, and shall also be liable to fine, under Section 103 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 [1].

- Section 101 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 defines murder and sets out the exceptions where culpable homicide is not murder [4].

- In case of a second or subsequent conviction under Section 303 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, the punishment shall be rigorous imprisonment for a term not less than one year and extending up to five years, with fine [1].
- In first-time conviction cases where the stolen property's value is less than five thousand rupees, the offender shall, upon returning the value of the property or restoring the stolen property, be punished with community service under Section 303 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 [1].

rows.question: How is a sale of immovable property defined and completed?
queries: How is a sale of immovable property defined and completed?
sale of immovable property definition transfer of ownership price paid or promised
Transfer of Property Act section 54 sale how made delivery of tangible immovable property
Transfer of Property Act section 55 rights and liabilities of buyer and seller
topSources: The Transfer of Property Act, 1882 s54

The Sale of Goods Act, 1930 s22

rows.answer:
A sale of immovable property is defined as a transfer of ownership in exchange for a price paid or promised or part-paid and part-promised, under Section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 [1]. As discussed by the Supreme Court in the judgment Lucknow Nagar Nigam & Others versus Kohli Brothers Colour Lab. Pvt. Ltd. & Others, to constitute a sale there must be a transfer of ownership from one person to another where all rights and interests possessed by a person are transferred with free consent for a price called consideration, and the transaction is complete and title passes only when the conveyance is regarded in accordance with law [11].

Conditions and time limits:
- In the case of tangible immovable property of the value of one hundred rupees and upwards, or a reversion or other intangible thing, the transfer can be made only by a registered instrument, under Section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 [1]. (Note: For the State of Assam, under the State Amendment to Section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, such transfer must be by an instrument registered in the State of Assam, notwithstanding anything contained in the Indian Registration Act, 1908 [1].)

rows.question: What is the punishment for identity theft using a computer?
queries: What is the punishment for identity theft using a computer?
punishment for identity theft using a computer or communication device

rows.answer:
The punishment for identity theft is imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three years and liability to a fine which may extend to rupees one lakh, under Section 66C of the Information Technology Act, 2000 [1].

Related provisions:
- Section 66D of the Information Technology Act, 2000 covers punishment for cheating by personation by using computer resource, punishable with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three years and a fine which may extend to one lakh rupees [3].
- Section 66B of the Information Technology Act, 2000 covers punishment for dishonestly receiving stolen computer resource or communication device, punishable with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three years or with fine which may extend to rupees one lakh or with both [4].

In first-time conviction cases where the stolen property's value is less than five thousand rupees, upon the return of the property's value or restoration of the stolen property, the offender shall be punished with community service under Section 303(2) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023. [1]
